source: original; documents are public-domain primary sources or paraphrases of them (see each document's sourcing note)

books.section: Topic 3.2 The Seven Years' War (The French and Indian War)

prompt: Evaluate the extent to which British policy toward the American colonies changed between 1754 and 1763.

documents.title: The Albany Plan of Union
documents.source: Benjamin Franklin, Albany Plan of Union, adopted by the Albany Congress, 1754. Public domain.
documents.sourcing: Franklin's plan for a colonial union, adopted by the Albany Congress in 1754. The plan was rejected by the colonial assemblies and by London.
documents.text: That the said general government be administered by a President General, to be appointed and supported by the Crown, and a Grand Council, to be chosen by the representatives of the people of the several Colonies met in their respective assemblies.

documents.title: Washington reports Braddock's defeat
documents.source: George Washington, letter to Governor Robert Dinwiddie of Virginia, July 1755. Paraphrased.
documents.sourcing: Washington, a Virginia provincial officer, writing to his governor days after General Braddock's defeat near Fort Duquesne. Paraphrased from the letter.
documents.text: Washington reported that the Virginia provincials had stood their ground and fought bravely at the Monongahela, while the British regulars broke and ran. He added that the colonial troops had borne the heaviest losses of the day.

documents.title: Pitt's circular letter to the colonial governors
documents.source: William Pitt, circular letter to the colonial governors, December 1758. Paraphrased.
documents.sourcing: Pitt, the British secretary of state directing the war, writing to the governors to secure colonial cooperation. Paraphrased from the circular letter.
documents.text: Pitt informed the colonial governors that Britain would send a large fleet and army to America in 1759, and that the Crown would repay the colonies for the cost of raising, clothing, and paying their own provincial troops.

documents.title: Treaty of Paris, Article IV
documents.source: Treaty of Paris, signed February 10, 1763. Public domain.
documents.sourcing: The peace treaty ending the Seven Years' War, stating the terms France accepted for North America.
documents.text: His Most Christian Majesty renounces all pretensions which he has heretofore formed or might have formed to Nova Scotia or Acadia in all its parts, and guaranties the whole of it, and with all its dependencies, to the King of Great Britain.

documents.title: Royal Proclamation of 1763
documents.source: Royal Proclamation of October 7, 1763. Public domain.
documents.sourcing: A royal order issued by George III, setting out how the newly enlarged empire would be governed and how Native lands would be treated.
documents.text: And whereas it is just and reasonable, and essential to our Interest, and the Security of our Colonies, that the several Nations or Tribes of Indians with whom We are connected, and who live under our Protection, should not be molested or disturbed in the Possession of such Parts of Our Dominions and Territories as, not having been ceded to or purchased by Us, are reserved to them, or any of them, as their Hunting Grounds.

documents.title: Gladwin reports from Fort Detroit
documents.source: Major Henry Gladwin, report from Fort Detroit, May 1763. Paraphrased.
documents.sourcing: Gladwin, the British officer commanding Fort Detroit, reporting to his superiors as Pontiac's warriors surrounded the fort. Paraphrased.
documents.text: Major Henry Gladwin reported that Pontiac and several hundred warriors had surrounded Fort Detroit, cut off its supplies, and demanded its surrender. Gladwin wrote that his garrison could hold only if relief reached Detroit from the east.

documents.title: The cost of the war
documents.source: Debt figures: UK Parliament historical national debt figures. Troop figures: 5 Steps to a 5, 2024, Chapter 9.
documents.sourcing: A table of the war's costs to Britain and the forces that fought it in North America, drawn from parliamentary records and the course books.
documents.text:
| Item | Figure |
| British national debt, 1754 | about £75 million |

rubric.criterion: Thesis: earns the point for a historically defensible claim that answers the prompt, stating the extent to which British policy changed between 1754 and 1763, with a clear line of reasoning.
rubric.notEarned: Restating the prompt with no claim about the extent of change does not earn the point.

rubric.criterion: Contextualization: earns the point for describing a broader historical context relevant to the prompt, such as salutary neglect before the war, the rivalry between Britain and France in North America, or the cost of the war to Britain.
rubric.notEarned: A sentence of background with no link to the argument does not earn the point.

rubric.criterion: Evidence from documents (first point): earns the point for describing specific and relevant evidence from at least three documents to support an argument about change or continuity in British policy.
rubric.notEarned: Using fewer than three documents, or quoting documents without describing what they show, does not earn the point.

rubric.criterion: Evidence from documents (second point): earns the point for using the content of at least six documents to support an argument, with the evidence accurately described and tied to the claim.
rubric.notEarned: Using fewer than six documents, or listing documents without connecting them to the argument, does not earn the point.

rubric.criterion: Evidence beyond the documents: earns the point for describing a specific and relevant example beyond the documents, such as the Sugar Act of 1764, the Stamp Act of 1765, or Pitt's reimbursement of colonial war costs.
rubric.notEarned: A general statement with no specific example beyond the documents does not earn the point.

rubric.criterion: Sourcing: earns the point for explaining the relevance of a document's author, purpose, audience, or historical situation to the argument, for at least two documents.
rubric.notEarned: Identifying an author without explaining why it matters, or sourcing only one document, does not earn the point.

rubric.criterion: Complexity: earns the point for demonstrating a complex understanding, such as qualifying the extent of change, explaining why change was uneven, or connecting the war years to the postwar order.
rubric.notEarned: A second example with no qualification or weighing does not earn the point.

modelOutline:
Thesis: British policy changed fundamentally between 1754 and 1763, from a loose empire that left the colonies largely to govern and tax themselves to an empire that planned, paid for, and then sought to control the continent — though the change was driven by war, not by a settled design.
Context: Before 1754 Britain practiced salutary neglect; the colonies ran their own assemblies and taxes while France hemmed them in from the west. The Ohio Valley clash forced London to take direct charge of the war.
Evidence: Documents 1-3 show the war years — colonial initiative in the Albany Plan, colonial sacrifice in Washington's letter, then Pitt's partnership with the assemblies. Documents 4-7 show the new order — conquest confirmed in the treaty, a settlement line drawn by the Proclamation, rebellion answered at Detroit, and a doubled debt.
Beyond the documents: Grenville's Sugar Act of 1764 and Stamp Act of 1765 carried the new policy into taxation, and colonial resistance followed within months.
Sourcing: Franklin's plan shows colonial thinking; Washington's letter shows the provincial experience; the Proclamation shows London's priorities, written by the king for his ministers.
Complexity: The change was real but uneven — Pitt's partnership years were cooperation, not control, and the postwar measures were improvisations to pay for victory, not a single design.
